title: OS Credential Dumping: DCSync
summary: DCSync abuses the directory replication protocol so that a host which is not a domain controller can ask a controller for password data as though it were another controller. The request uses the normal replication interface, so the controller answers with hashes for the accounts named in the request, including highly privileged accounts and historical entries. The rights needed are those held by administrators or granted through replication permissions, which makes permission review the primary control rather than network filtering. The distinguishing artefact is a replication request that originates from a workstation or member server instead of a genuine controller, usually generated by a process that is not the directory service itself. Detection pairs rights auditing with directory service and network logs, because the exchange can otherwise look entirely routine.

beginner.definition: Domain controllers copy data between each other using a built-in process called replication. DCSync pretends to be a domain controller and asks for password data. The request uses a normal interface, so it can be hard to tell apart from real copying. This differs from the parent because nothing is read from local memory or files.
beginner.whyItMatters: It can steal the most powerful accounts in the domain. No malicious file needs to run on the domain controller itself. The request looks like normal copying between controllers. Recovered hashes can be used to forge logins for a long time. Reviewing who may copy directory data is your strongest control.
howItWorks: Domain controllers share data using a built-in copying process called replication.
The attacker obtains an account that is allowed to ask for directory data.
A tool on an ordinary machine sends replication requests to a controller.
The controller replies with password hashes for the accounts requested.
The attacker repeats the requests for high value and historical accounts.
The stolen hashes are used later to sign in or to forge access tokens.
beginner.example: Picture a company where branch managers send stock requests to head office. Head office answers any request that carries a valid manager badge. A thief copies a manager badge and asks head office for the complete staff file. The request looks like ordinary business and is answered without question. DCSync is that copied badge, and the staff file is the password data.
takeaways: Replication rights are powerful, so review who holds them regularly.
A replication request from an ordinary computer is a strong warning sign.
Rotate the most privileged accounts if you suspect this activity.

objectives: Explain what directory replication is and why DCSync abuses it.
Describe which account rights make this technique possible.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the credential dumping parent.
Identify evidence of replication requests from non controller systems.
Explain why stolen privileged hashes support long term access.
